links.passage: Evidence from smart-agriculture field application indicates that soil-moisture-sensor guidance can improve irrigation efficiency and support water savings relative to conventional approaches, reinforcing the case for sensor-anchored scheduling as a practical route to improved WUE (Adak, 2025).

links.section: 6.3 Decision Rules and Stress Timing: Linking Analytics to Water-saving Strategies

links.passage: Because extreme rainfall and heat can disrupt intended wet–dry cycles, digital monitoring—ranging from simple field thresholds to sensor-based tracking—helps keep AWD within safer bounds and enables re-wetting before stress crosses yield-damaging thresholds (Carrijo et al., 2017).
supporting_passages: In rice systems, alternate wetting and drying (AWD) exemplifies this integration: mild AWD can save water while maintaining yields across many contexts, whereas severe drying increases water savings but raises the risk of yield penalties (Carrijo et al., 2017).
Consequently, AWD implementation for CSA should be adaptive, guided by soil water thresholds and seasonal risk rather than fixed calendars (Carrijo et al., 2017).
links.inference_note: The sensor-based tracking refers to monitoring soil water thresholds in AWD (as stated in 5.5), and the paper claims it enables re-wetting before yield-damaging stress occurs, thereby protecting yield.
reference_entries: Carrijo, D. R., Lundy, M. E., & Linquist, B. A. (2017). Rice yields and water use under alternate wetting and drying irrigation: A meta-analysis. Field Crops Research, 203, 173–180. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fcr.2016.12.002
links.section: 6.3 Decision Rules and Stress Timing: Linking Analytics to Water-saving Strategies

links.passage: Digital systems can operationalise this by combining crop stage awareness with short-range weather patterns and soil moisture trends to decide when a deficit remains acceptable and when it becomes risky.
supporting_passages: The core principle is to maximise production per unit of water consumed or applied by allowing controlled deficits while protecting highly sensitive stages, recognising that yield penalties can become disproportionate once critical thresholds are exceeded (Fereres & Soriano, 2007).
links.inference_note: The paper states that data-driven digital scheduling systems operationalise deficit irrigation, whose cited core principle is maximising production per unit of water, so the scheduling decision delivers the water-productivity gain.
reference_entries: Fereres, E., & Soriano, M. A. (2007). Deficit irrigation for reducing agricultural water use. Journal of Experimental Botany, 58(2), 147–159. https://doi.org/10.1093/jxb/erl165

links.passage: Advances in remote sensing have expanded the feasibility of estimating ET across large areas and over time, and a recent review of remote sensing and AI approaches highlights rapid progress in satellite data, preprocessing pipelines, and machine-learning workflows that can scale ET estimation (Fong et al., 2025).
supporting_passages: First, they can reveal spatial heterogeneity in water use and crop stress within and between fields, which supports targeted water allocation when supplies are limited.
links.inference_note: The cited sentence names satellite remote sensing for ET estimation, and the following paragraph states that these ET products support targeted water allocation when supplies are limited (delivery control).
reference_entries: Fong, T. Y., Huang, Y. F., Chin, R. J., & Koo, C. H. (2025). Advancing evapotranspiration estimation with remote sensing and artificial intelligence – A review. Agricultural Water Management, 322, 110023. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agwat.2025.110023
